title: Low-rank approximation and Eckart–Young
subtitle: G2 lecture 053000 · expanded mathematical companion
adaptation: Standalone companion adapted from the source spoken lecture and display-only mathematics appendix. Explicit hypotheses, stepwise proofs, worked examples, and local vector diagrams; no narration edits.

slides.title: The best approximation with only k directions
slides.lead: A rank-k map can send every input into at most a k-dimensional output subspace.
body: Given A:E→F, we want the best such approximation in either operator norm or Frobenius norm. The singular-value decomposition gives a canonical candidate by retaining the k largest singular-value terms.
The Eckart–Young theorem proves this truncation is optimal even among competitors that choose completely different source and output directions.
slides.takeaway: Keep the strongest singular directions to minimize either worst-case or total squared error.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 053000 · The best approximation with only k directions

slides.title: Truncate the singular-value decomposition
slides.lead: Write A=∑σ_i u_i v_i* with descending positive singular values.
body: Define A_k by keeping only the first k terms. Its rank is at most k because its range lies in span(u₁,…,u_k). The error A−A_k is the sum of all discarded singular pieces.
Orthogonality of the singular vectors lets us compute both error norms directly from the omitted values.
slides.takeaway: The truncated SVD is an explicit rank-k competitor with computable error.

slides.title: Worst-case error of the truncation
slides.lead: The operator norm measures the largest error over unit input vectors.
body: The discarded part has singular values σ_{k+1},σ_{k+2},…; hence its operator norm is the largest discarded value σ_{k+1}.
To prove optimality, let B have rank at most k. Its kernel intersects the span of the first k+1 right singular vectors nontrivially. On a unit vector in that intersection, Bx=0 and ‖Ax‖≥σ_{k+1}.
slides.takeaway: Every rank-k map misses an input with stretch at least σ_{k+1}.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 053000 · Worst-case error of the truncation

slides.title: The Frobenius error
slides.lead: The Frobenius norm measures the total squared output lengths over an orthonormal input basis.
body: The rank-one singular pieces are orthogonal in the Frobenius inner product. Therefore the squared norm of the discarded tail is the sum of the squares of the discarded singular values.
For the truncated SVD the error is exactly the square root of that sum. The difficulty is showing an arbitrary rank-k competitor cannot improve it.
slides.takeaway: Squared Frobenius error adds the energy of every discarded singular direction.

slides.title: Why an arbitrary rank-k map cannot do better
slides.lead: Let R=ran B for any competitor B with rank at most k, and let P_R be its orthogonal projection.
body: For every input x, the error A x−B x contains a perpendicular component (I−P_R)Ax, so its squared norm is at least that component’s squared norm.
Summing over an orthonormal input basis gives ‖A−B‖_F²≥‖(I−P_R)A‖_F². The latter is minimized by choosing R to capture the k strongest left singular directions.
slides.takeaway: Projection onto the competitor’s range isolates error that no rank-k output can remove.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 053000 · Why an arbitrary rank-k map cannot do better

slides.title: Finish the squared-error lower bound
slides.lead: For any output projector P_R of rank at most k, the captured squared Frobenius energy is bounded by the top k singular squares.
body: Indeed ‖P_R A‖_F²=tr(P_R A A*) and Ky Fan’s maximum principle bounds this trace by ∑_{i≤k}σ_i².
Subtract from the total energy ∑_iσ_i². The resulting residual is at least ∑_{i>k}σ_i², and the truncated SVD attains equality.
slides.takeaway: Ky Fan energy capture gives the matching Frobenius lower bound.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 053000 · Finish the squared-error lower bound

slides.title: A three-by-three numerical example
slides.lead: Let A=diag(5,2,1), and keep only its largest singular value.
body: The rank-one truncation A₁=diag(5,0,0) leaves diag(0,2,1). Its operator-norm error is 2; its Frobenius error is √(4+1)=√5.
For rank two, A₂=diag(5,2,0) leaves error 1 in both norms. These examples show why operator and Frobenius errors can differ while sharing the same optimal truncated SVD.
slides.takeaway: Operator error is the largest omitted singular value; Frobenius error adds all omitted squares.

slides.title: Tied singular values and nonuniqueness
slides.lead: An optimal rank-k approximation may not be unique when the truncation boundary lies inside a repeated singular-value space.
body: For A=diag(3,3,1) and k=1, keeping either of the first two coordinate directions yields the same operator-norm error 3 and the same Frobenius error √10.
More generally, rotations within a repeated singular-value subspace can produce distinct optimal truncations. The optimal error values remain intrinsic even when the approximating map is not unique.
slides.takeaway: Degeneracy affects the optimizer but does not change the best achievable error.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 053000 · Tied singular values and nonuniqueness

slides.title: Rectangular and exact-rank cases
slides.lead: The theorem applies to any finite-dimensional linear map, not just square matrices.
body: A rectangular A:E→F still has an SVD with source singular vectors and output singular vectors. Truncating to k nonzero terms gives a map of rank at most k with the same error formulas.
If k≥rank A, the truncation equals A and the optimal error is zero. Thus the theorem is consistent with exact reconstruction when all nonzero singular directions are retained.
slides.takeaway: Eckart–Young handles rectangular maps and vanishing tails automatically.

slides.title: Rebuild both optimality arguments
slides.lead: The proofs use different measurements but one shared candidate: the truncated SVD.
body: For operator norm, intersect ker B with the top k+1 right singular span and obtain a worst-case unit vector. For Frobenius norm, project A onto ran B and use Ky Fan’s trace bound for captured energy.
The two lower bounds match the explicit errors of A_k. This proves optimality without restricting competitors to share A’s singular bases.
slides.takeaway: The candidate comes from the SVD; dimension counting and energy capture prove no competitor does better.
